query: Which method can be used for concurrent strength–ductility improvement, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a quenching and partitioning (Q&P) heat treatment with carefully controlled temperatures will yield simultaneous increases in strength and ductility by stabilizing retained austenite for transformation-induced plasticity.
generation.material_initial_state: A fully austenitized medium-carbon steel prior to quenching.
generation.intervention: Perform a Q&P procedure: rapidly quench from the austenitizing temperature to a temperature between the martensitic start (Ms) and finish (Mf), then elevate and hold at a chosen partitioning temperature to stabilize retained austenite.
generation.conditions: Precise quench temperature slightly above Mf, followed by partitioning (e.g. 200–400 °C) for controlled durations.
generation.structural_mediator: Retained austenite stabilized within a predominantly martensitic matrix.
generation.mechanism: Retained austenite undergoes strain-induced transformation during deformation, providing additional plasticity and enhancing fracture resistance while maintaining high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventionally quenched and tempered steels, the Q&P-treated alloy will exhibit higher strength accompanied by an observable improvement in ductility.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties of the same steel after traditional quenching and tempering processes.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness varies with steel composition, austenitizing conditions, and specific quenching/partitioning parameters. Over- or under-partitioning can reduce the retained austenite fraction and diminish property gains.
generation.uncertainty: The exact partitioning temperature and duration needed to maximize retained austenite stability may vary among different steel grades, requiring further experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical steel batches, apply the Q&P treatment at different quenching and partitioning temperatures, and compare mechanical properties to a traditionally quenched and tempered control.
measurements: Volume fraction of retained austenite via X-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no measurable increase in both strength and ductility is observed relative to the quenched-and-tempered control, then the hypothesis is disproved.
